The founder allele induces yeast cell death; depletion of the fly ortholog impairs respiration and ATP production. These support a conserved cellular-injury branch, with different perturbations and assay systems.

PAM16 links mitochondrial import to skeletal development, but the human tissue intermediates and any additional MAGMAS functions remain unresolved. Mouse expression and the human genetic skeletal phenotype support an ossification hypothesis, not a directly measured growth-plate import lesion.

edges.description: Conserved MAGMAS effects on cellular respiration provide a proposed myocardial injury route. The human cardiac phenotype and mouse cardiac expression support tissue relevance, but patient myocardial ATP loss has not been demonstrated.
Reduced vertebral-body ossification and growth is a proposed explanation for the marked vertebral flattening. No patient vertebral histology establishes the responsible cellular lesion.

Disordered metaphyseal growth and modeling is proposed to produce the widened distal femoral contour. The radiograph establishes widening, while the link to the proposed ossification defect remains indirect.
Impaired endochondral bone formation is proposed to reduce longitudinal growth of the long bones. The authors support an ossification role, but do not measure growth-plate dynamics in patients.
Impaired skeletal growth is proposed to limit rib elongation. The specific rib growth-plate lesion has not been demonstrated.
Restricted growth of the short-ribbed, narrow thorax could limit lung expansion. This is a proposed mechanical contribution; the clinical series does not exclude intrinsic lung disease.
Abnormal modeling of the rib ends is proposed to produce the cupped contour. The clinical rib appearance does not establish a specific chondrocyte or osteoblast defect.
Reduced thoracic skeletal growth is proposed to limit chest width. The sources do not partition the contributions of rib length, rib orientation and vertebral development.
Uneven thoracic skeletal growth is a candidate explanation for the bell-shaped contour. The authors’ broad ossification hypothesis does not establish the regional growth pattern responsible.
Disordered pelvic bone growth and modeling is proposed to alter iliac proportions. No patient tissue study identifies how the squared contour develops.
Abnormal pelvic growth and modeling is proposed to alter acetabular roof orientation. The horizontal roof is documented radiographically; its cellular origin remains unresolved.
Disordered acetabular modeling is proposed to generate the trident configuration. This extrapolates the authors’ skeletal hypothesis and does not establish a specific developmental intermediate.
Reduced pelvic bone development is proposed to impair ischial growth. The available sources establish hypoplasia but not its cellular mechanism.

Abnormal vertebral growth and modeling is proposed to reduce lumbar pedicle spacing. The source does not establish whether reduced ossification or another developmental process determines that spacing.
Disordered longitudinal skeletal growth is proposed to contribute to proximal limb shortening. The reason for disproportionate proximal involvement remains unexplained.
Impaired longitudinal skeletal growth is proposed to reduce limb length disproportionately. This qualified skeletal route does not account for every component of systemic growth failure.
Impaired bone elongation is proposed to contribute to reduced linear growth after birth. The broader growth phenotype could also reflect nutrition, systemic illness or other mitochondrial functions.
Proposed myocardial energetic injury could produce cardiomyopathy; its occurrence is established clinically, but the specific energetic attribution is not.
Thoracic restriction can compromise ventilation; its contribution to the reported respiratory insufficiency is inferred from the skeletal anatomy.
Respiratory insufficiency caused the first-family girl's death at nine months.
Respiratory insufficiency caused the first-family boy's death around age two.
Myocardial disease was associated with severe cardiac enlargement in the affected siblings; enlargement is a manifestation of the cardiomyopathy.
The clinically reported cardiomyopathy culminated in fatal pump failure in the second family.
Heart failure caused death around age two in both second-family siblings.
Atlantoaxial subluxation narrowed the upper cervical canal in this patient.

The authors associate this patient’s cervical instability and myelopathy with hypotonia, supporting a possible contribution from cord compromise. Hypotonia decreased during follow-up before cervical surgery, while spasticity increased. The authors also call the hypotonia central without localizing it further; central includes the spinal cord. The relation does not establish ongoing compression, exclude other central or developmental contributors, or explain hypotonia in the earlier founder families.

Cervical myelopathy is a qualified contributor to the survivor’s spastic diparesis. Pyramidal signs preceded cervical surgery; repeat MRI at six years ten months showed no compression or instability, but spastic diparesis was still present at thirteen years. This is not a demonstrated continuously reversible effect of ongoing compression. Residual injury from earlier cord compromise and other central contributors remain possible; the report does not distinguish their contributions.
Upper cervical canal narrowing provides the anatomical route to the subsequently reported cord compression; progression and dynamic instability are not separately quantified.
The human disease allele, expressed in place of the yeast ortholog, reproduces the import block that this node asserts.
edges.limitations: Yeast has no growth plate, no cardiomyocyte and no vertebral column, so the model speaks only to the conserved import chemistry and can say nothing about how that chemistry becomes a skeletal disease. The defect is also only expressed at non-physiological temperatures, so the assay reports a conditional phenotype rather than the constitutive one patients carry at 37 degrees.

nodes.description: The only in vivo animal work on this gene family that bears on the disease mechanism. Black-pearl is the Drosophila ortholog of MAGMAS/Pam16. Depleting it depolarises mitochondria, drops ATP by 60 per cent, raises reactive oxygen species 3.5-fold and selectively cuts cytochrome c oxidase activity by 65 per cent; in hypomorphic larvae, plasmatocyte number and mitochondrial staining fall and N-acetylcysteine doubles viability, which is the strongest evidence that ROS is a causal effector rather than a bystander. It is not a model of the disease: the allele is a knockdown or hypomorph rather than the human missense change, and flies have no endochondral skeleton.

nodes.description: PAM16-associated dysplasia impairs skeletal ossification and modeling, producing short and abnormally shaped bones. Molecular and tissue links upstream of this node remain provisional.

evidence.snippet: Structurally, the Gln74Pro mutation introduces a proline, which would certainly disrupt helix71–84.

nodes.description: Saccharomyces cerevisiae pam16-delta strains were complemented with wild-type or p.Asn76Asp human MAGMAS. Mutant growth was preserved at 28 degrees, slowed at 34 and absent at 36, particularly on non-fermentable medium. Nonpermissive conditions revealed Hsp60 precursor accumulation, reduced mutant protein, fragmented mitochondria and pexophagy. This establishes a conditional allele effect in yeast, without explaining human survival or predicting clinical responses to temperature.
